title: Idempotence: An 1870 Algebra Term Describes Terraform's Core Promise
explainer: In 1870, mathematician Benjamin Peirce circulated 'Linear Associative Algebra' (initially a small lithographed edition for colleagues; it wasn't formally published in a journal until 1881), coining the term 'idempotent' for an algebraic expression that gives the same result no matter how many times it's applied - formally, A squared equals A. Terraform's central value proposition - that running 'terraform apply' repeatedly against an unchanged configuration converges to, and then stays at, the same infrastructure state - is this exact algebraic property applied to infrastructure. Recognizing idempotence as a precise, 19th-century mathematical idea (rather than just an IaC buzzword) clarifies why a well-written configuration is safe to re-run, while one with side effects, like a provisioner that always appends a line to a file, is not.

title: CFEngine (1993): The Original 'Describe the State You Want' Tool
explainer: In 1993, Mark Burgess, then at the University of Oslo, wrote CFEngine to replace brittle, host-specific shell and Perl scripts with a single declarative file describing what a fleet of Unix machines should look like; re-running it converged any machine toward that described state rather than re-executing a fixed sequence of commands. This 'declare the desired state and let the tool reconcile it' philosophy - which CFEngine pioneered roughly a decade before Puppet and Chef, both founded by former CFEngine users - is the same philosophy Terraform applies to cloud infrastructure instead of individual servers.
